### Project Story
This project grew out of more than three years of sustained engagement by Upper Arlington Rotary in the Lake Atitlán region — six separate club delegations totaling over 1,000 volunteer hours — giving the team unusually strong ground-level knowledge before the grant was even written. The trade school was conceived as a natural progression from the club's earlier support of a local middle school, recognizing that basic education alone was insufficient without vocational pathways. The grant was authorized and implemented as planned through 2014, with no reported changes to objectives. However, the financial reporting raises a significant flag: both the progress report (February 2015) and the final report (May 2016) show **zero expenses logged against the full 569,853 GTQ budget**, with the entire budget appearing as variance — suggesting that expense documentation was not entered into the Rotary reporting system, even though supporting financial spreadsheets were attached. Despite this administrative gap, the final report records 726 direct beneficiaries — a remarkable outcome that far exceeded projections — and the grant was accepted and closed. Long-term stewardship of the school was handed to Mayan Families, which had the organizational capacity and community relationships to sustain the programs independently.

- Upper Arlington Rotary had invested **255+ Rotary Days / 1,000+ volunteer hours** in Guatemala before this grant, making it one of the club's most deeply relationship-based international efforts.

## GG1415576 — Potable Water for Multiple Communities
*Global Grant · 2015–2017 · Lake Atitlán region, Guatemala*

---

### What We Did
This project installed Sawyer in-line water filtration systems in public primary schools and Mayan Families-operated preschools across multiple rural communities surrounding Lake Atitlán, Guatemala. Alongside the physical infrastructure, the project delivered a WASH (water, sanitation, and hygiene) education curriculum to students and parents, including hygiene training, group handwashing stations, wash basins, soap drives, and oral hygiene supplies. The goal was to create a lasting, low-maintenance source of safe drinking water while building community knowledge and demand for clean water practices.

---

### Community Served
Rural indigenous Mayan communities around Lake Atitlán, Sololá Department, Guatemala — a population of over 250,000 dependent on a rapidly polluting lake, facing high rates of diarrheal disease, gastritis, and stomach cancer linked to contaminated water. The final report recorded **5,276 direct beneficiaries**.

---

### Budget
| Item | Amount |
|------|--------|
| Total grant / project budget | $37,610 USD (GTQ 259,793) |
| Rotary Foundation World Fund match | $15,870 USD |
| District Designated Funds (District 7950) | $10,000 USD |
| Club cash contributions (Hingham & Hull RC) | $11,740 USD |

---

### Partner Organizations

**Rotary Clubs**
- Rotary Club of Hingham (& Hull), District 7950 — *International sponsor* (Massachusetts, USA — North American)
- Rotary Club of Lake Atitlán, District 4250 — *Host sponsor* (Guatemala)

**NGOs & Local Organizations**
- **Mayan Families** (Panajachel, Sololá, Guatemala) — primary implementing partner; managed procurement, community outreach, filter installation, and education programming. A Gold Star GuideStar recipient and multiple-year Top Nonprofit awardee; more than 80% indigenous Mayan staff.
- **Sawyer / Bombagua** — water filter supplier (Guatemala City distribution)
- **Government of Guatemala** — project aligned with the national *Healthy Schools* initiative for school sanitation standards

---

### Key Personnel
- **August Muller** — International primary contact, Rotary Club of Hingham, District 7950
- **William Boegel** — Host primary contact, Rotary Club of Lake Atitlán, District 4250
- **Emilio Crespo Morales** — Host secondary contact, Lake Atitlán RC
- **Sidney Eschenbach** — Host secondary contact, Lake Atitlán RC
- **David Powers** — International secondary contact, Hingham RC
- **Carolyn Kennedy** — International secondary contact, Hingham RC
- **Dewitt Delawter** — Hingham RC; authorized both grant reports (2016, 2017)
- **Dwight Mara-Poage** — Lake Atitlán RC; authorized both reports
- **Gregory Roche** — DRFC, District 7950 (Bourne-Sandwich RC)
- **Carlos Andrade Morales** — DRFC, District 4250 (Guatemala Norte RC)

---

### Outcomes
- **5,276 people** directly benefited from the project (per final report)
- Sawyer in-line water filters installed across multiple public primary schools and Mayan Families preschools within 6 months of project launch; filters rated for **10-year service life**
- Group handwashing stations and wash basins installed in participating schools
- WASH education curriculum developed (2-month development phase) and delivered to students throughout the full school year
- Parent education workshops conducted with incentives for participation
- Soap drive conducted; toothbrushes, toothpaste, and hygiene supplies distributed to students
- Local teachers trained to maintain filters (backflow cleaning); Mayan Families designated as ongoing technical support and replacement-parts liaison
- Water filter ownership transferred to local town governments (primary schools) and Mayan Families (preschools) — no Rotary ownership of assets
- Project aligned with Guatemala's national *Healthy Schools* government initiative

---

### Project Story
This project was proposed and funded in 2014–2015 with a clear, well-structured plan backed by a credible and experienced local partner in Mayan Families. The filters were to be installed within six months and education programming run for a full school year, with the entire project concluding by March 2016. In practice, the project ran significantly longer than planned — the progress report was authorized in mid-2016 and the final report not until early 2017, suggesting roughly a one-year delay beyond the original timeline. A notable financial transparency concern appears in both reports: the expense log shows **zero recorded expenditures** against a GTQ 259,793 budget, with the entire budget listed as variance — this likely reflects a reporting system limitation or the fact that Mayan Families managed funds directly and detailed line-item entries were not entered into the Rotary portal, though supporting receipts and bank documents were uploaded as attachments. Despite these documentation gaps, both reports were accepted by the Foundation, and the final report confirmed 5,276 beneficiaries served — more than double the 2,500+ originally projected. The long-term sustainability plan was sound: durable Sawyer filters, trained local teachers, a Water Committee maintenance plan, and Mayan Families as an ongoing community anchor all positioned the project for continued impact well beyond the grant period.

---

### Notes
- Mayan Families received the **Rotary World Service Above Self Award (2012)** and multiple **Top Nonprofit awards from GreatNonProfits.org (2010–2013)** — an unusually well-credentialed cooperating organization.
- The international contact (August Muller) had a prior personal relationship with the community, having supported an indigenous family in the area for several years before proposing the grant — providing strong contextual grounding for project design.
- Several authorizations were still listed as "needed" at grant close (Brian Sullivan, Michael Rosen, José Interiano Torre, Stephen Albright), which may warrant follow-up for records completeness.

*Global Grant · 2015 · Rural communities, Departments of Sololá and Suchitepéquez, Guatemala*

### What We Did
This project supported 137 indigenous Mayan young women — 59 active high school seniors on track to become the first in their families to graduate, and 78 recent graduates — through scholarships, weekly mentorship meetings, family support visits, vocational training, entrepreneurial development, and professional internships. The program aimed to break cycles of poverty by building economic autonomy, job readiness, and access to critical systems such as banking, healthcare information, and communications. ### Community Served

This project was built on genuine, multi-year Rotary engagement: seven members of Greeley Centennial had visited the Starfish site in Guatemala, met students and families, and delivered computers and supplies before the grant was even filed — a strong foundation. ## GG1526219 — Mayan Power and Light
*Global Grant · 2015–2017 · Lake Atitlán Region, Guatemala*

---

### What We Did
The project trained 60–75 young Mayan women in electricity, circuits, and solar power through "Circuits and Solar" workshops, then supported graduates in launching women-owned solar businesses. Two small businesses were established — one in Panajachel/Sololá and one in Chicaco near Santiago Atitlán — to sell and install affordable solar systems for domestic use. The broader goal was to break cycles of poverty by combining technical education with business incubation.

---

### Community Served
Rural and peri-urban Indigenous Mayan communities around Lake Atitlán, Guatemala — one of the poorest regions in the western hemisphere — where many households lacked access to electrical power or could not afford grid connection costs.

---

### Budget
| Item | Amount |
|------|--------|
| Total grant budget | $40,500 USD |
| Rotary World Fund match | $17,142 USD |
| District 5080 DDF | $10,929 USD |

### Partner Organizations

**Rotary Clubs:**

- **SEA – Soluciones/Sistemas Energeticas Apropiadas** (Quetzaltenango) — primary technical partner; training, curriculum, hardware supply and warehouse management
- **ATC – The Appropriate Technology Collaborative** (San Marcos la Laguna) — curriculum development, business incubation, project management, five-year hardware commitment
- **Asociación Estrella de Mar / Starfish One by One** (Panajachel) — women's empowerment partner; originally a cooperating org but withdrew during implementation
- **CECAP** — Guatemalan trade school providing workshop space

---

### Key Personnel
- **Ted Steacy** — International primary contact, Nelson Rotary Club, District 5080
- **Dwight Mara-Poage** — Host primary contact, Lake Atitlán Rotary Club, District 4250
- **John Barrie** — Project director, day-to-day management of Mayan Power and Light program
- **Sidney (Sid) Eschenbach** — Host secondary contact; document review and progress oversight
- **Sharon Smart** — Host secondary contact, Lake Atitlán
- **Bob Hargreaves** — International secondary contact; in-country liaison in Guatemala during project
- **Colleen Driscoll** — International secondary contact, Nelson
- **Norma Bayan** — Starfish One by One program director (named in application narrative)
- **John Ferguson** — Nelson Rotary Club; authorized both progress and final reports
- **William Boegel** — Lake Atitlán Rotary Club; authorized both progress and final reports
- **Norman McCarvell & Vlad Sasarman** — DDF authorizations, District 5080

---

### Outcomes
- **11,399 people** reported as directly benefiting from the project (final report)
- Training delivered to **50–99 individuals** (women trained in circuits and solar — target was 60–75)
- **1–19 businesses** supported (two women-owned solar businesses launched)
- **20–49 jobs created** through the new solar enterprises
- **500–999 solar lighting installations** completed in rural homes
- Electronics curriculum revised and printed; teaching materials, solar hardware kits, and demonstration equipment procured
- Two "Circuits and Solar" workshops taught (21 days each)
- Business incubation workshops completed; businesses officially registered
- SEA retained ownership of solar hardware inventory; graduates sold products on consignment, avoiding startup debt
- ATC committed to a five-year hardware installation support relationship

---

### Project Story
The Mayan Power and Light project was rooted in genuine community co-design: it grew from conversations between ATC, Starfish One by One, and local Guatemalan trade school CECAP, with women mentors specifically requesting that job pathways be added to the technical curriculum. Implementation ran longer than the original January 2015–January 2016 window, extending into early 2017, primarily because solar hardware was delayed in Guatemalan customs — a common logistical challenge in the region. A more significant change was the withdrawal of Starfish One by One as a cooperating organization mid-project; this was disclosed to The Rotary Foundation and approved, with ATC and SEA absorbing the program delivery roles. The financial reporting in both the progress and final reports shows zero expenses logged in the online system despite supporting receipts being uploaded separately, suggesting the Rotary online portal was not used for detailed transaction entry — an administrative gap, though the grant was accepted by TRF in both instances. The lasting handoff was structural: SEA owns the solar product inventory, the women's businesses operate on consignment, and ATC's five-year commitment provides an ongoing technical backstop — a sustainability model designed to outlast the grant itself.

---

### Notes
- The consignment model (women entrepreneurs sell from SEA's inventory without taking on debt) was a deliberate design choice to reduce financial risk for participants in a very low-income context.
- The reported beneficiary figure of 11,399 likely reflects households and community members reached through solar installations, not just the women directly trained.
- The application noted plans to engage Rotaract clubs from Nelson, BC and Ann Arbor, MI — no further mention of their participation appears in the reports.
- Both the progress and final reports were authorized by substitute sponsors (John Ferguson and William Boegel) rather than the original primary contacts (Ted Steacy and Dwight Mara-Poage), suggesting leadership transition within the sponsoring clubs during the project period.

## GG1526673 — X-ray Machine & Mini C-Arm Fluoroscopy for San Lucas Toliman Hospital

*Global Grant · 2014–2017 · San Lucas Toliman, Guatemala*

---

### What We Did
This project purchased and installed two critical pieces of medical imaging equipment at Hospital Obras Sociales de Monsignor Gregorio Schaffer in San Lucas Toliman, Guatemala: a full-body CR digital X-ray system and a portable mini C-arm fluoroscopy machine. The CR system replaced a failed analog X-ray machine and eliminated the need for film and chemical processing, while enabling digital image transmission for remote specialist consultation. The mini C-arm was intended primarily for intraoperative use during orthopedic and podiatric surgeries, but also for emergency and bedside imaging.

---

### Community Served
The hospital serves over 34,000 people in the remote Mayan region around Lake Atitlán — the only low-cost care facility in the area, as the nearest government hospital requires a 2–3 hour ambulance ride.

---

### Budget

| Item | Amount |

| Total project budget | $94,479 |
| World Fund (Rotary Foundation) match | $40,491 |
| District 5050 DDF contribution | $26,994 |
| Fidalgo Island Rotary Club (cash) | $26,994 |

> **Note:** The expense log in both the progress and final reports shows $0 in recorded expenditures against the full $94,479 budget, with the entire amount listed as variance. Financial supporting documents (bank statements, receipts, customs fee summaries) were uploaded as attachments but their contents are not reproduced in the report text.

---

### Partner Organizations

**Rotary Clubs & Districts:**

- Fidalgo Island Rotary Club, District 5050 *(North American — primary cash contributor and mission team club)*
- Lake Atitlan Rotary Club, District 4250 *(Host sponsor — Guatemala)*

- **Sedecal** (Spain) — equipment supplier for the CR X-ray system, spare parts, software, installation, warranty, and technician training

### Key Personnel

| Dwight Mara-Poage | Lake Atitlan RC; host secondary contact; authorized progress and final reports |

### Outcomes

- **1,352 people** reported as directly benefiting from the project (recorded in the final report)
- CR digital full-body X-ray system procured from Sedecal (Spain) and installed at the hospital
- Mini C-arm fluoroscopy machine (XiScan, refurbished) procured and installed for surgical, ER, and bedside use
- Hospital X-ray technician trained on new equipment; on-site training provided by manufacturer
- Spare parts and local service arrangements established through a Guatemala-based Sedecal representative
- Digital imaging capability enabled remote transmission of X-ray images to specialists in the US, Spain, and elsewhere
- Elimination of analog X-ray film, chemical developers, and film storage requirements
- Ongoing annual podiatric/orthopedic surgical missions by Dr. Miller's team supported by intraoperative fluoroscopy
- Equipment ownership transferred to the hospital (non-profit); no Rotarian ownership

> **Caveat on measurement data:** While six impact measures were defined at application (monthly X-ray counts, patients assessed, health professionals trained, children under 5 treated, etc.), the "Results to Date" fields in both the progress and final reports appear blank in the available documents. Quantitative outcome data beyond the 1,352 beneficiary figure was not captured in the report text.

---

### Project Story

This project addressed an urgent and concrete crisis: the hospital's only X-ray machine had failed before the February 2014 surgical mission, forcing Dr. Miller's team to improvise with an old portable unit brought from the US. The application was well-grounded — equipment had been selected, vendors quoted, and the need verified through years of direct mission experience dating to 2011. The project ran from November 2014 through April 2015 as planned, with equipment shipped from Spain, cleared through Guatemalan customs, and installed on-site with manufacturer training. However, the financial reporting raises questions: both the progress report (mid-2016) and the final report (mid-2017) show zero recorded expenditures in the expense log despite the full $94,479 budget, suggesting either a reporting system limitation or incomplete data entry — though supporting bank statements and receipts were uploaded as attachments and the reports were accepted by the Foundation. The lasting impact is credible: a busy hospital serving 34,000+ underserved Guatemalans gained modern digital imaging capabilities that directly supported ongoing surgical missions and everyday clinical care, with local ownership, trained staff, and a maintenance budget already in place.

## GG1633934 — Namaste Business Development & Microloans, Boca Costa Region

*Global Grant · 2016–2020 · Suchitepequez & Solola Departments, Guatemala*

---

### What We Did
This project provided microcredit loans, entrepreneurial training, and one-on-one business advisory support to low-income women entrepreneurs in rural and semi-rural communities of the Boca Costa region of Guatemala. Implemented through Fundacion Namaste Guatemaya (FNG), participants received financial literacy training and individualized business coaching every 28 days alongside loan disbursements tied to personal business plans. The goal was to move women from extreme poverty toward sustainable economic self-sufficiency.

---

### Community Served
Rural and semi-rural indigenous Mayan women in Suchitepequez and Solola Departments, Guatemala — a population with extremely high poverty rates, limited formal education, and no access to fair credit — supporting 101+ women entrepreneurs and their families.

---

### Budget

| Item | Amount |
|------|--------|
| Total grant budget | $66,028 |
| Rotary Foundation (World Fund match) | $31,024 |
| District 5150 DDF contribution | $28,024 |
| Club cash contributions (Mill Valley, Marin Evening, Pacifica RC) | $6,000 |
| Non-Rotarian contribution (St. Aidan's Episcopal Church, SF) | $980 |
| Project income generated (interest & fees from borrowers) | $20,283 |

---

### Partner Organizations

**Rotary Clubs:**
- Pacifica Rotary Club, District 5150 *(International sponsor — Northern California)*
- Lake Atitlan Rotary Club, District 4250 *(Host sponsor — Guatemala)*
- Mill Valley Rotary Club, District 5150 *(Financial contributor — Northern California)*
- Marin Evening Rotary Club, District 5150 *(Financial contributor — Northern California)*

**NGOs & Local Organizations:**
- **NamasteDirect / Fundacion Namaste Guatemaya (FNG)** — implementing MFI; recruited and screened borrowers, delivered all training and advisory services, maintained individual financial records
- St. Aidan's Episcopal Church, San Francisco *(non-Rotarian donor)*

---

### Key Personnel

| Name | Role |
|------|------|
| Patrick Hall | International primary contact, Pacifica RC |
| William Boegel | Host primary contact, Lake Atitlan RC |
| Dwight Mara-Poage | Host secondary contact, Lake Atitlan RC |
| Emilio Crespo Morales | Host secondary contact, Lake Atitlan RC |
| Steven Wright | International secondary contact, Pacifica RC |
| Wendy Santiago | International secondary contact, Pacifica RC |
| Linda Jonas | International secondary contact, Pacifica RC |
| Eugenia Duran | Financial manager, Fundacion Namaste Guatemaya |
| James Renfro | Legal agreement signatory, Pacifica RC |
| John Van Lente | Sponsor authorization, Lake Atitlan RC |
| Armand Boissy | Sponsor authorization, Lake Atitlan RC |
| Carl Schwab | Sponsor authorization, Pacifica RC |

---

### Outcomes

- **104 women** directly benefited from the project (exceeding the original target of 101)
- **Cycle 1:** 69 women received 5½ hours of financial training and 9 individual advisory visits — totaling **981 individual advisory visits**
- Average **business profit increase of $197** per participant during first loan cycle
- **84% of borrowers** learned to keep business records for sales and expenses — remarkable given that **one-third were illiterate**
- Participants ranged in age from 20–69; **93% were classified in the "extremely vulnerable" poverty range**
- Average microloan disbursed: **$347 per borrower**
- **32 additional clients** approved for microloans only (second cohort); all recruitment and training activities for both cohorts completed by August 2019
- Project generated **$20,283 in income** from borrower interest and fees, retained for continued lending
- All 9 planned project activities completed; final evaluation concluded August 2019

---

### Project Story
The project launched in late 2017 — over a year after the grant application was authorized in August 2016 — suggesting administrative or disbursement delays before implementation began. The midpoint progress report (2018) showed all activities still "in progress" with 69 of the intended 101 participants enrolled in the first cycle and funds flowing primarily through the Training category rather than the separate Operations/Microloans line, resulting in a significant budget variance (Training overrun of ~GTQ 158,000; Operations underspent by GTQ 171,014). The sponsors reported this variance was due to interest earned from loan repayments, and elected not to return unused funds to the Foundation — indicating those funds were recycled into further lending, which is consistent with a revolving microcredit model. By the final report (March 2020), the project was declared complete with all activities finished and 104 total beneficiaries served, slightly exceeding the original goal. The partnership with FNG proved durable: FNG had previously implemented two other Global Grants with Rotary clubs in Guatemala, and the Lake Atitlan club confirmed the program model was well-suited to the region's needs.

---

### Notes
- FNG was simultaneously implementing two other Rotary Global Grants at the time of this application (GG1421211 and GG1413365), reflecting a long-standing Rotary–Namaste partnership across Guatemala.
- The project's revolving loan structure meant grant funds continued generating community benefit beyond the grant period through reinvested interest income ($20,283 reported).
- The Pacifica–Lake Atitlan partnership was originally introduced by Namaste Direct in fall 2014; formal planning meetings occurred in April 2016 before the grant was submitted.

## GG1865581 — Young Mayan Women as Engines of Economic Growth in Guatemala

*Global Grant · 2018–2020 · Sololá, Guatemala*

---

### What We Did
This project funded the launch and development of Colegio Impacto ("Impact School"), a middle and secondary school operated by Asociación Estrella de Mar (EdM) for indigenous Mayan girls in rural Guatemala, emphasizing STEM education, critical thinking, information technology, and 21st-century workforce skills. Grant funds supported teacher training and coaching, purchase of computers and library books, standardized assessment systems, and an economic empowerment program ("Quetzal Fund") for recent high school graduates that included English training, internships, small-business incubation, university tutoring, and leadership summits. Best practices were shared with at least 29 partner organizations and public schools across Guatemala through EdM's Chispa Network.

### Community Served
Indigenous Mayan girls and young women in the Department of Sololá, Guatemala — a population that is 96% indigenous, where 81% of youth live in poverty, nearly 60% of girls aged 15–19 are married or mothering, and girls historically discontinue schooling after 6th grade.

---

### Budget

| Item | Amount |
|------|--------|
| Total grant | $162,150 |
| Rotary Foundation (World Fund match) | $70,300 |
| District Designated Funds (DDFs) | $48,750 |
| Club cash contributions | $43,100 |

---

### Partner Organizations

**Rotary Clubs & Districts (North American unless noted):**
- Rotary Club of Evergreen, District 5450 — *International Sponsor*
- Rotary E-Club of Lake Atitlán (RECLA), District 4250 — *Host Sponsor*
- Denver, Westminster 7:10, Westminster, Mountain Foothills of Evergreen, Golden, Conifer, Parker, Highlands Ranch (Littleton), Denver Tech Center, Boulder, Littleton, Greeley (Centennial), Fort Collins-Breakfast, Billings, Novato, Lacey — Districts 5450, 5440, 5390, 5020
- Districts 5440, 5390, 5020 (DDFs)

**NGOs & Local Organizations:**
- Asociación Estrella de Mar / MAIA-Impact (implementing organization, Panajachel)
- Teachers 2 Teachers Global (STEM teacher coaching)
- ConTextos, El Salvador (critical thinking and literacy)
- Pomona Impact / Pomona AgTech (entrepreneurship coaching)
- Universidad del Valle de Guatemala / ACCESS English Program
- Starfish One-by-One (U.S. 501(c)3 affiliate of EdM)
- Child Aid, INTECAP, JUCONI (Mexico), WINGS, She's the First, Girl Rising, Ajchowen, Women's Justice Initiative, Speak!, Wuqu Kawok, Namaste, 1bot — training and outreach partners

---

### Key Personnel
- **Alan Steger** — Rotary Club of Evergreen, International Primary Contact
- **William (Will) Boegel** — RECLA, Host Primary Contact; founder of Opal House Guatemala
- **Theodore (Ted) Ning** — RC Evergreen, founder of Starfish One-by-One; 20+ years in Sololá
- **Travis Ning** — Executive Director, Starfish One-by-One; founding RECLA member
- **Norma Bajan** — Director, Asociación Estrella de Mar (twice invited to the White House)
- **Mercedes Alvarado** — Director of Finances, Estrella de Mar
- **John Van Lente, Mayra Tobías** — RECLA, Secondary Contacts/Host Committee
- **Robert Rose, Jim Kreider** — RC Evergreen, International Committee
- **Manolo Saloj** — Technology Coordinator, Colegio Impacto
- **Hjungjoon Jin** — Professional Development Specialist

---

### Outcomes

- **437** young women accessed secondary school through Colegio Impacto (school grew from 1 class of 47 in 2017 to ~150–200 students in grades 7–9 by 2019)
- **197** female students exceeded one year of academic growth in math and literacy (MAP/Lexile assessments)
- 9th-grade MAP math scores improved by ~2 grade levels per school year; average 7th-grade Lexile score rose from 288 (2018) to 544 (end of 2019)
- **50 laptops** and related equipment (tablets, projectors, charging stations) installed in technology lab; library stocked with 200+ books
- **9 educators** received 1,276 hours of professional development in 2019 alone
- **650** teachers/practitioners from public schools and NGOs attended STEM or critical thinking summits
- **500** public school teachers/NGO representatives trained in critical thinking and literacy (ConTextos modules)
- **44** "Girl Pioneers" (recent graduates) completed an 8-month ACCESS English program (2018 and 2019)
- **40** recent graduates completed internships in formal businesses and NGOs
- **27** graduates completed the small-business incubator; **8 small businesses** launched and operating
- **76** emerging female leaders attended annual leadership and networking summits
- **91** participants earning income in excess of Guatemala's average income
- **25** Girl Pioneers achieved full economic independence; 17 in formal employment
- **2** Girl Pioneers graduated from university; **44** currently enrolled with 98% retention
- **29+ organizations** across Guatemala trained in Colegio Impacto's innovative practices
- Only **15 of 227 program graduates (7%)** are mothers, versus a national average of 50% by age 21

---

### Project Story
The project launched on time in mid-2018, but immediately began evolving beyond its original scope in productive ways: the new Colegio Impacto building was inaugurated in November 2018, triggering a rapid expansion from 100 to over 200 students that drove higher-than-budgeted equipment costs. Two planned activities were cancelled or restructured — weekly entrepreneurship coaching (Activity 1) was dropped when outside funds covered it, and in-person Guatemala City mentoring sessions (Activity 7) were folded into the broader leadership summit program (Activity 15) — and those savings were redirected with host club approval into expanded IT equipment, library resources, and extended internship and coaching programs that proved highly effective. Budget variances were significant: equipment overspent by ~Q61,000 GTQ and project management by ~Q99,000 GTQ (due to additional coordinators hired), while training and supplies came in under budget; total expenditures exceeded the grant budget by Q33,817 GTQ, which Estrella de Mar covered from its own funds. Financial management was transparent throughout, with a dedicated Banrural account, monthly reporting to RC Evergreen, and dual oversight by RECLA — and all reporting was submitted and accepted by the Rotary Foundation. The lasting impact was substantial: Colegio Impacto became a recognized regional hub for girl-focused educational innovation, training 29+ Guatemalan organizations, receiving international media attention (BBC documentary), and earning recognition at the ZAYED Sustainability Prize in Abu Dhabi — establishing a self-sustaining model that EdM (now rebranded MAIA-Impact) continues to operate and expand.

---

### Notes
- This was the **third consecutive Rotary Global Grant** in partnership with Estrella de Mar, building on GG1426078 and GG1525485. The long relationship between RC Evergreen and EdM (dating to 2010, with 150+ Rotarian visitors) was central to the project's success.
- Potential conflicts of interest were proactively disclosed: Ted Ning (RC Evergreen) founded Starfish One-by-One, the U.S. affiliate of EdM, and his son Travis was RECLA's founding member; neither held a direct administrative role in this grant.
- Asociación Estrella de Mar rebranded as **MAIA-Impact** during the grant period.
- A Rotary Cadre of Technical Advisors site review (Cecelia Babkirk, 2015) called the EdM program "absolutely my favorite" of all cadre reviews conducted — a testament to the organization's quality that carried into this grant.
- The Chispa Network grew from 10 to over 18+ member organizations, and at least one partner organization (Horizontes Sin Límites, Chajul) began opening its own school modeled on Colegio Impacto.

narrative:
## GG1867690 — Water & Sanitation for Nuevo Progreso and Chocol

*Global Grant · 2018–2021 · Santa Lucía Utatlán, Sololá, Guatemala*

---

### What We Did
This project delivered potable water infrastructure and wastewater treatment systems to two underserved villages — Nuevo Progreso and Chocol — in the uppermost municipality of the Lake Atitlán watershed. In Nuevo Progreso, the team dug wells, installed a hilltop holding tank, piped water to 96 families and an elementary school, constructed a school septic system, and replaced 37 substandard latrines. In Chocol, five small septic systems were installed serving groups of 5–10 homes each, with one system used to conduct research on plant species effectiveness in drain-field filtration.

---

### Community Served
Two villages in Santa Lucía Utatlán, Sololá, Guatemala — Nuevo Progreso (originally 45 families plus a regional school; expanded to 96 families serving ~1,200 people) and Chocol (17 families; ~225 people) — lacked reliable potable water and any meaningful wastewater treatment, with untreated waste flowing directly into the Lake Atitlán watershed.

---

### Budget

| Item | Amount |
|------|--------|
| Total grant | $82,250 USD |
| Rotary Foundation (World Fund match) | $37,125 USD |
| District Designated Funds (Districts 5960 & 4740) | $29,125 USD |
| Club cash contributions (Northfield, Watsonville, Red Wing) | $16,000 USD |

---

### Partner Organizations

**Rotary Clubs & Districts:**
- Northfield Rotary Club, District 5960 *(North America — international sponsor)*
- Lake Atitlán Rotary Club, District 4250 *(host sponsor)*
- Watsonville Rotary Club *(financial contributor)*
- Red Wing Rotary Club *(financial contributor)*
- District 4740 *(DDF contributor — Brazil)*

**NGOs & Local Organizations:**
- **Asociación Pro Agua del Pueblo (ADP)** — primary implementing partner; provided all engineering, construction supervision, community education, and financial record-keeping
- **Engineers Without Borders – Guatemala** — site inspections and technical feedback on construction
- **Mil Milagros** — hygiene and water/sanitation education in schools and with women in both communities
- **COCODEs** (community village councils) — local governance bodies that took ownership of systems post-completion

---

### Key Personnel

- **Todd Thompson** (Northfield RC) — international primary contact; chemist and teacher; traveled to Guatemala twice for water testing and oversight
- **Terrence (Joe) Wakely** (Lake Atitlán RC) — host primary contact; resident in Guatemala; led day-to-day implementation and financial management
- **Mayra Tobías** (Lake Atitlán RC) — host secondary contact; environmental attorney
- **Jack Bower** (Lake Atitlán RC) — host secondary contact
- **Ragh Singh & Charles Cogan** (Northfield RC) — international committee members
- **Erick Tok** — original Director, Agua del Pueblo (monitoring & evaluation)
- **Juanita Hernandez** — successor Director, Agua del Pueblo (mid-project)
- **Carlos Simon** — final Director/lead engineer, Agua del Pueblo (project close-out)

---

### Outcomes

- ✅ Potable water system installed serving 96 families + school (~1,200 people) in Nuevo Progreso
- ✅ One primary well dug and a second assisted; hilltop holding tank installed; distribution piping to 91+ homes and school
- ✅ Septic system constructed at Nuevo Progreso elementary school; functional bathrooms established
- ✅ 37 substandard latrines replaced in Nuevo Progreso
- ✅ 5 small septic systems installed in Chocol (serving 5–10 homes each); one used for plant-species drain-field research
- ✅ Rainwater drainage and collection tank added at school for dry-season supply
- ✅ 2 functioning community governance committees (COCODEs) established with tariff/usage-fee structures in place
- ✅ ~350 days of volunteer labor recorded; ~10 individuals formally trained
- ✅ Full budget of 600,421 GTQ (~$82,250 USD) expended with zero variance at close
- ✅ Community contracted to provide all unskilled labor; ongoing maintenance funded through water-use fees

---

### Project Story
The project launched in April 2018 and was originally scoped for two years, but ultimately ran through May 2021 — a roughly one-year extension driven in part by the COVID-19 pandemic, which delayed financial reporting and slowed construction in the final phase. Scope actually *expanded* rather than contracted: Nuevo Progreso grew from 45 to 96 families served, and the school septic system and 37 latrine replacements were added. The first progress report (mid-2019) showed meaningful infrastructure in place but only 848 direct beneficiaries and just 3 individuals formally trained — well short of goals — reflecting how long community water projects take to reach full operation. By final report (August 2021), all activities were marked complete, all funds were fully expended with no variances, and 1,200 people had direct access to improved water. Leadership of the implementing partner, Agua del Pueblo, turned over twice during the grant (Erick Tok → Juanita Hernandez → Carlos Simon), which required ongoing relationship management but did not derail the work. The COCODE governance structure and usage-fee system provide a credible sustainability mechanism, and the project is explicitly framed as a first step toward serving the entire Lake Atitlán watershed of 430,000 people.

---

### Notes
- This grant is positioned as the opening phase of a long-term watershed-wide initiative across 19 municipalities in Sololá; a prior related grant (GG1529575) is referenced in the application.
- One of the Chocol septic systems was used as a small research installation studying which plant species most effectively filter wastewater in drain fields — an unusual scientific value-add for a humanitarian grant.
- District 4740 (Brazil) contributed DDF funds ($4,125), reflecting an international multi-district partnership beyond the standard two-club model.

description: COVID-19 medical equipment and supplies for three community healthcare providers in Alameda County, CA.
narrative:
## GG2013637 — Area 4 COVID-19 Community Healthcare Response
*Global Grant · 2020–2021 · Hayward, Castro Valley, Dublin, Pleasanton, and Livermore, California, USA*

---

### What We Did
This project provided COVID-19-prioritized medical equipment and supplies to three community healthcare providers in California's Alameda County, responding directly to formal equipment requests from each provider. In parallel, Rotarian volunteers were engaged to support COVID-19 contact tracing and community outreach and education initiatives. The grant also enabled Rotarian volunteers to physically deliver over 280 blood pressure home-monitoring units to patients on behalf of Axis Community Health.

### Community Served
Vulnerable and underserved residents of Alameda County, California — including Medi-Cal, uninsured, and low-income patients served by federally qualified community health centers and a regional trauma center — who faced heightened COVID-19 risk and reduced access to care.

---

### Budget
| Item | Amount |
|------|--------|
| Total grant | $96,850 |
| Rotary Foundation (World Fund match) | $48,425 |
| District 5170 DDF contributions | $48,425 |
| Club cash contributions | Not stated |

---

### Partner Organizations

**Rotary Clubs**
- Rotary Club of Livermore — District 5170 (host, North America)
- E-Rotary Club of Lake Atitlan — District 4250 (international partner, Guatemala)
- Rotary Club of Hayward — D5170
- Rotary Club of Castro Valley — D5170

**NGOs & Local Organizations**

- Asian Health Services (Alameda Health Consortium member, Hayward)
- Eden Medical Center / Sutter Health (Castro Valley; only Level-2 trauma center in Tri-Valley)
- Alameda Health Consortium / OCHIN (procurement and EHR compatibility infrastructure)
- Tri-Valley Non Profit Alliance
- California Department of Public Health / UCSF / UCLA (contact tracing training context)

---

### Key Personnel
- **Patrick Coyle** — Host primary contact, Rotary Club of Livermore (pat@coyles.com)
- **Armand Boissy** — International primary contact, E-Rotary Club of Lake Atitlan
- **Glenn D. Kubiak** — Host committee, financial manager/treasurer, RC Livermore
- **Jeffrey Youngsma** — Host committee, RC Livermore
- **Terrence Wakely** — International committee, RC Lake Atitlan
- **Mayra Tobías** — International committee, RC Lake Atitlan
- **Carolyn Siegfried** — Club President, RC Livermore (authorized payments)
- **Ken Perine** — Sponsor authorization, RC Livermore
- **Russell Hobbs** — DRFC Chair, D5170 (RC Santa Cruz); authorized DDF and grant
- **Marcelo Coyi** — DRFC Chair, D4250 (RC Belize)
- **Ramesh Hariharan** — DDF authorization, RC Silicon Valley Passport, D5170
- **Kathleen Jose Le** — Eden Medical Center contact (joselek@sutterhealth.org)
- **Darren Yee** — Asian Health Services contact (dyee@ahschc.org)
- **Valerie Jonas** — Axis Community Health contact (vjonas@axishealth.org)

---

### Outcomes
- **62,760 people** directly benefited from disease prevention interventions (against an initial target of 2,500+)
- **$15,000** reimbursed to Eden Medical Center for a GlideScope intubation device, reducing physician exposure during intubation
- **$5,098** reimbursed to Asian Health Services for fingertip pulse oximeters and digital blood pressure monitors
- **$76,752** reimbursed to Axis Community Health for: 584 in-home monitoring devices (BP monitors, glucose meters, cardiometers, scales, pulse oximeters integrated with Epic EHR); 30 smart no-touch thermometers; 54 telehealth headsets for clinical staff; an ID NOW immunity testing machine; a vaccine refrigerator; CareSignal subscription; and electronic health records support
- **280+ blood pressure monitoring units** hand-delivered to Axis Community Health patients by Rotarian volunteers, saving approximately $10/unit in packaging and shipping
- **17 volunteers** engaged in COVID-19 outreach and support initiatives (against an initial target of 2,500+)
- Press release issued; coverage in local/regional print and online media and the D5170 TRF Newsletter
- Virtual briefing sessions conducted with each healthcare provider, recorded and shared with Area 4 Rotary clubs
- All funds fully expended; zero budget variance; no unused funds returned

---

### Project Story
This project launched efficiently during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, with community health care providers identified and formal equipment requests received within weeks of the grant's inception in April–May 2020. Equipment payments to Eden Medical Center and Asian Health Services were completed by August 2020, but the largest disbursement — to Axis Community Health — was not finalized until June 2021, reflecting the complexity of procuring and configuring OCHIN-compatible EHR-integrated devices. The volunteer engagement component fell well short of its ambitious 2,500+ target, ultimately enrolling only 17 volunteers for outreach initiatives; this likely reflects the difficulty of formalizing volunteer pipelines during a fast-moving pandemic when government agencies stood up their own contact tracing infrastructure. The project's most tangible community touchpoint beyond equipment was the Rotarian-led delivery of 280 blood pressure units to Axis patients — a visible, hands-on partnership that saved the clinic real costs and gave club members direct service engagement. All grant funds were fully spent with no variances, the final report was accepted, and ownership of all equipment transferred permanently to the healthcare providers, who continue to operate and maintain it under their own established programs.

---

### Notes
- The actual scope of the Axis Community Health reimbursement ($76,752) differed from the original line-item budget (which totaled ~$76,752 across four separate Axis budget lines), suggesting some reallocation within the Axis allocation — notably, the final report references a vaccine refrigerator and CareSignal subscription not listed in the original application. The total remained exactly $96,850 with no net variance.
- The E-Rotary Club of Lake Atitlan (Guatemala) served as the international partner primarily for communication and knowledge-sharing purposes; no funds flowed internationally, as the entire project was implemented in California.
- The grant was funded entirely through D5170 DDF matched 1:1 by the Rotary Foundation World Fund; no club cash fundraising was required.

title: Water, Sanitation, Hygiene for Vista Hermosa, Phase II
narrative:
## GG2578692 — WASH for Vista Hermosa, Phase 2

*Global Grant · 2026–2027 · Vista Hermosa, Santa Lucia Utatlan, Solola, Guatemala*

---

### What We Did
Phase 2 built on a concurrent potable water project (Phase 1, GG2570516) by installing modular wastewater treatment plants (MWWTPs) and sanitation infrastructure for every household and the regional school in the village of Vista Hermosa. Each MWWTP serves clusters of up to ten homes and combines household collector sewers, grease traps, community collection tanks, two-stage septic treatment, and a constructed biological wetland that produces safe irrigation-quality effluent. The project also delivered a ten-session hygiene and system-maintenance training program for the entire community.

---

### Community Served
Vista Hermosa is a small, steep-terrain Mayan agricultural community in the municipality of Santa Lucia Utatlan, Solola, Guatemala, serving 49 households and one regional school whose residents faced severe gastrointestinal illness, open wastewater runoff, and no functional sanitation system.

### Outcomes

*Intended outcomes — no completion reports available at time of writing.*

- Installation of **5 residential MWWTPs**, each serving up to 10 homes (up to 50 households total)
- Installation of **1 school MWWTP** serving the regional school
- **Topographical and environmental impact studies** completed pre-construction
- **100–499 individuals** trained in system governance, operation, maintenance, and hygiene (10 consecutive Friday sessions)
- **Community Water & Sanitation Committee** trained and operational as ongoing governance body
- Treated effluent reused safely for **household irrigation**, reducing pressure on potable supply
- Stabilized septic sludge made available as **agricultural fertilizer** for local farmers
- Long-term funding secured via **signed community tariff plan** covering all 49 beneficiary households
- mWater application adopted for ongoing **monitoring and evaluation**

---

### Project Story

Only the grant application is available; no interim or final reports have been filed. The project is the direct sequel to Phase 1 (GG2570516), which restored potable water to Vista Hermosa, and was designed from the outset with the understanding that increased water supply would make wastewater management the village's next critical need. The partnership between RC Annapolis and RC Lake Atitlan traces to their first meeting at the 2017 Rotary International Convention in Atlanta, deepening through several joint grants over nearly a decade. Agua del Pueblo, whose co-founder Bruce Clemens is an RCLA member (a disclosed but managed conflict of interest), brings 53 years of Guatemala rural WASH experience and has already deployed eight comparable MWWTP systems in the region, making the technical approach well-validated. Project execution is scheduled July 2026 – July 2027; the municipality of Santa Lucia Utatlan has expressed intent to replicate the MWWTP model across other villages.

---

### Notes

- **Conflict of interest formally disclosed:** Bruce Clemens co-founded Agua del Pueblo in 1972 and served as president through 1980; he has received no remuneration from AdP since 1977 and serves only in an advisory capacity. Rotary reviewed and accepted this disclosure.
- **Phase linkage:** This grant cannot be fully evaluated in isolation — its success depends on Phase 1 (GG2570516) delivering reliable water supply; the water committee and sanitation committee are the same body.
- **Replication potential:** Municipal leaders visited an existing AdP MWWTP site during community assessment and confirmed interest in using Vista Hermosa as a regional template.
- **Technology note:** Systems are gravity-fed, require no electricity, and are designed for community self-maintenance — a deliberate sustainability choice for a low-income, steep-terrain setting.
